lesson.title: What You Know Versus What You Might Learn: Achievement and Aptitude Tests
lesson.summary: Achievement tests measure what a person has already learned, while aptitude tests aim to predict future learning or performance, though the two overlap more than the labels suggest.
lesson.body:
Standardized tests, covered in an earlier chapter, are often sorted into two broad purposes that are easy to state in principle but sometimes blurry in practice: achievement tests and aptitude tests. An achievement test is designed to measure what a person has already learned or mastered up to this point, typically tied to a specific curriculum or body of content. A final exam in a psychology course, a state mandated reading test for fourth graders, and a certification exam for a licensed profession are all achievement tests in this sense: they look backward at material the test taker was expected to have already learned.

An aptitude test, by contrast, is designed to look forward, aiming to predict a person's capacity to learn or perform in the future rather than to certify what they already know. The Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery, used to help place military recruits into roles suited to their strengths, is a clear example, since it is meant to forecast future performance in various job categories rather than test mastery of content those recruits have necessarily already studied.

College admissions tests occupy an interesting and somewhat contested middle ground in this distinction. The SAT was originally developed and marketed under the name Scholastic Aptitude Test, reflecting an intention to measure general reasoning ability related to future college performance rather than mastery of a specific high school curriculum. Over time, however, the test's name and framing shifted away from the word aptitude, partly in response to a recognition that performance on this kind of test is not a pure, curriculum free measure of innate potential. It also reflects accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, and skills built up through years of schooling and life experience, which are exactly the kinds of things an achievement test is designed to capture.

This overlap is not really a flaw unique to college admissions testing. It reflects the earlier point, from the chapter on the g factor, that fluid and crystallized intelligence are related but distinguishable, and that most real world cognitive performance draws on both prior learning and more general reasoning capacity at the same time. In practice, the achievement versus aptitude distinction is best understood as a difference in intended purpose and interpretation rather than a perfectly clean separation of test content. An achievement test is judged mainly by its content validity, meaning how well it covers what was supposed to be taught, while an aptitude test is judged mainly by its predictive validity, meaning how well it actually forecasts the future outcome it claims to predict, both concepts introduced in the earlier chapter on test validity.

Teachers, counselors, and employers still find the distinction useful in practice, even if it is not perfectly clean in theory. Reporting a student's achievement scores tells a school what that student has mastered so far and where gaps in learning remain, which supports decisions about placement, remediation, or advancement within an existing curriculum. Reporting an aptitude score, by contrast, is meant to support a forward looking decision, such as whether a person is likely to succeed in a course of study or job role they have not yet attempted, which is a fundamentally different kind of question even when the two kinds of tests end up looking fairly similar on the page.
